title: Hierarchical entropy-aware KV compression probe (runtime fidelity controller)
creator: Diego Morales
description:
Goal: Evaluate a hierarchical, entropy-aware KV compression strategy with an in-runtime fidelity controller that dynamically switches between FP8/INT8/INT4 encodings per KV shard to maximize GPU memory savings while bounding generation-quality regressions.

Motivation: Prior KV quantization probes have shown per-shard sensitivity and non-uniform degradation across tokens and cohorts. Instead of single-mode quantization (int8 across the board) we hypothesize that a hierarchy of encodings (lossless-ish FP8 for hot shards, int8 for warm, int4 for cold) plus an entropy metric and small runtime controller will reduce memory by >35% with <1.5% quality regression on targeted prompt cohorts.

Success criteria:
- Peak GPU KV memory reduction >= 35% on eval model (redwood-large-v1) for typical chat workloads.
- End-user quality regression (ROUGE-L / perplexity / top-k accuracy on eval prompts) <= 1.5% absolute versus baseline FP16 KV.
- Latency P95 regression <= 10ms for generation paths where controller is active.
- No unexplained model crashes or silent divergence after 24h stability run.

Design summary:
1) Shard scoring: compute per-shard entropy and L2 magnitude sketch during warmup. Use a lightweight running sketch (exponential moving average) stored in host memory.
2) Encoding tiers:
   - Tier A (hot): FP8 hybrid (8-bit with scaled exponent) for minimal fidelity loss.
   - Tier B (warm): Symmetric INT8 with per-shard scale and bias correction table.
   - Tier C (cold): Blocked INT4 with 16-value lookup and optional residual compensation for top-k queries.
3) Runtime fidelity controller: policy engine that chooses tier per shard based on entropy threshold, recent hit-rate, and available GPU memory. Controller is implemented as a non-blocking async task within the serving runtime and must not add blocking synchronizations on the request path.
4) Fallback/guardrails: if quantized shard causes token-level anomaly (sudden spike in token logits variance or repeated UNK tokens) controller instantly escalates to higher tier for that shard for N requests and reports metric.

Experiment plan:
- Phase 1 (microbench): implement encoding/decoding kernels and per-shard scoring; run unit perf tests on devbox A100 for correctness and throughput.
- Phase 2 (workload sweep): run synthetic prompt cohorts (chat short, long-context summarization, code) across redwood-large-v1 and redwood-xl-v1 to measure memory/quality tradeoffs.
- Phase 3 (stability): 24h continuous generation with live traffic replay (production-sampled traces) to monitor degradation and controller oscillation.
- Phase 4 (canary): small percentage canary in runtime-1.20 with tracing enabled in staging.

Datasets and cohorts:
- Internal eval suite (1.2k prompts) including user chat traces, long-context documents, code completion, and instruction-following tasks.
- Open-source benchmarks: HumanEval subset for code fidelity; CNN/DailyMail subset for summarization metrics.

Metrics collected:
- Memory: peak KV bytes, average KV bytes, memory fragmentation heuristics.
- Quality: token-level KL divergence, perplexity, ROUGE-L, pass@1 for code, top-3 exact token match.
- Perf: token latency p50/p95/p99, controller decision latency.
- Stability: oscillation count (controller thrashing), fallback frequency.

Implementation notes:
- Use existing KV shard abstraction in runtime (ShardID + host metadata map). Avoid changing model binary layout.
- Reuse kernel selection infra for packing/unpacking; add a small decoding stub that runs on copy-to-GPU to decode FP8->FP16 or INT4->INT8->FP16 as required.
- For INT4 blocked encoding, experiment with 64-element blocking vs 128-element blocking to balance decode throughput vs compression ratio.

Acceptance: if success criteria met in Phase 3 we will prepare a canary rollout (Phase 4) and a runtime-1.20 opt-in flag for Dedicated customers.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: controller oscillation causing jitter in latency. Mitigation: add hysteresis and minimum hold-time per shard.
- Risk: unexpected quality cliff for specific cohorts. Mitigation: cohort-aware holdout and immediate escalation with automated alerting to SRE.
- Risk: decode CPU overhead on host during copy-to-GPU. Mitigation: microbench and move to GPU-assisted decode if necessary.
results_summary:
Phase 1 completed: implemented kernels and per-shard scorer. Microbench shows correct decoding with these observed numbers on A100 devbox:
- Baseline FP16 KV: peak 12.3GB KV
- Tier A (FP8-hybrid median): 9.6GB KV (22% reduction), quality delta ~0.2%
- Tier B (INT8): 7.4GB KV (40% reduction), quality delta ~0.9%
- Tier C (INT4-blocked): 5.8GB KV (53% reduction), quality delta ~2.8%
Controller prototype toggled tiers without blocking and added ~3ms median decision latency. Early finding: int4 blocks occasionally exhibit high variance on code-completion prompts; residual compensation reduces error by ~0.7% but increases decode cost by ~0.6ms/token. Overall, combined hierarchical policy with entropy threshold targeting 60% Tier B, 30% Tier A, 10% Tier C achieved ~38% memory reduction with ~1.1% quality regression in short-chat cohort during synthetic sweep.
